title: Microsoft’s Quantum Chief Doesn’t Care That Scientists Don’t Believe His Results
gist: Microsoft quantum VP Zulfi Alam openly dismisses scientific peer review as too slow, refuses to share raw data behind Microsoft's Majorana-qubit claims citing commercial sensitivity, and is betting the company's credibility on shipping a working quantum computer by 2029 rather than winning over skeptics now — a strategy rival D-Wave's chief development officer reads as a tacit admission the results can't withstand scrutiny.

insights.claim: Zulfi Alam, Microsoft's corporate vice president of quantum, says he does not care that many scientists disbelieve the company's claim to have split an electron into Majorana quasiparticles, and refuses to share the raw underlying data, citing commercial sensitivity.
insights.speaker: Zulfi Alam
insights.so_what: A major public company is explicitly prioritizing IP protection over scientific verification for a multibillion-dollar technology bet, meaning outside investors and partners cannot independently validate the core technical claims underpinning Microsoft's quantum roadmap.
insights.locator: But Alam, Microsoft's corporate vice president of quantum

insights.claim: Alam argues that traditional peer review is too slow for the current pace of AI-accelerated research, noting a paper published in Nature in June was based on work completed two years earlier, and says he doesn't believe there are enough qualified experts to speed up the review process.
insights.speaker: Zulfi Alam
insights.so_what: Signals a broader industry tension in AI-accelerated science: companies may increasingly bypass or deprioritize peer review as a validation mechanism, shifting the burden of proof from publication to product delivery — a pattern investors should watch for across deep-tech startups making unverified breakthrough claims.
insights.quote: The world has changed in two years, so this notion of having peer reviews and publications doesn't work in this fast-moving world right now. That's why this paper thing is kind of boring now.
insights.locator: He also complains that the publishing process is too slow

insights.claim: In 2021, Microsoft retracted a quantum computing paper from Nature that had claimed evidence of Majorana particles, after independent physicists identified issues in the data analysis — the same underlying research area as last year's disputed breakthrough claim.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Microsoft's Majorana research program has a track record of walked-back claims, which should raise the evidentiary bar for any new unverified announcements from the same team and lower confidence in near-term timeline claims.
insights.locator: In 2021, Microsoft retracted a quantum computing paper

insights.claim: In June, Microsoft said it had produced a qubit 1,000 times more reliable than its predecessor using the company's own scientific-discovery AI agent, but scientists remain skeptical of the underlying Majorana work because Microsoft still won't share the raw data.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: A claimed 1,000x reliability jump is a headline-grade metric for Microsoft's quantum roadmap, but it rests on an unverified physical foundation (Majorana quasiparticles), so the figure should be treated as unconfirmed until independent data review occurs.
insights.locator: In June, the software giant said it had produced a qubit

insights.claim: Trevor Lanting, chief development officer at Nasdaq-listed rival quantum computer maker D-Wave Quantum, says the field has enough outside experts to reliably assess claims, and interprets a company's refusal to submit to scrutiny as an implicit admission that 'our results aren't strong enough to stand up to that scrutiny.'
insights.speaker: Trevor Lanting (via Isabella Ward)
insights.so_what: A direct competitor publicly casts doubt on Microsoft's evidentiary rigor, which is a useful signal for investors comparing quantum computing players' credibility — D-Wave itself has also faced accusations of inflating claims, per the article, so this rivalry framing should be read with that caveat.
insights.quote: so when a company or group says they don't have time, I would read that as 'our results aren't strong enough to stand up to that scrutiny.'
insights.locator: Having claims evaluated by science is

insights.claim: Majorana quasiparticles were first hypothesized nearly 90 years ago and have proved elusive to conclusively produce and observe, and Microsoft's approach — while theoretically promising — has been the company's longest-running research project and has been repeatedly plagued by controversy.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: The multi-decade difficulty and Microsoft's own history of retraction suggest the technical risk on Microsoft's topological qubit approach remains unusually high compared to competing qubit architectures (neutral atoms, charged atoms, light) being pursued by other firms.
insights.locator: While Microsoft's approach is theoretically promising

insights.claim: Rather than trying to win over skeptical scientists now, Alam says Microsoft plans to prove its Majorana-based approach by delivering a working, useful quantum computer, which the company has said it expects to achieve by 2029.
insights.speaker: Zulfi Alam
insights.so_what: 2029 is the concrete milestone against which Microsoft's quantum bet should be tracked; if the company continues withholding data while missing that date, it would substantially undercut the credibility of its Majorana claims.
insights.quote: Get this machine up and let the machine do the work.
insights.locator: Alam still doesn't think he needs to prove his work

insights.claim: Quantum computers are being pursued by multiple tech powerhouses and startups because they could theoretically solve currently-impossible problems in fields like drug development and defense, with parallel concerns that they could eventually be used to break current encryption standards.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Frames the commercial and strategic stakes (drug discovery upside, encryption-breaking risk) that justify the scale of investment and secrecy around quantum programs like Microsoft's, relevant background for assessing sector-wide quantum computing investment theses.
insights.locator: The goal for these companies is to create computers
